blocks.text: I can describe the properties of graphene and fullerenes, relating them back to their structures.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A different structural form of an element, e.g. graphite and diamond are allotropes of carbon.
An allotrope of carbon consisting of a sheet that is one-atom-thick. Each atom is covalently bonded to three others arranged in hexagonal rings.
A molecular allotrope of carbon. Each atom is covalently bonded to three others, forming nanoparticles with hollow spheres or tubes.
A spherical fullerene composed of 60 carbon atoms (held together by covalent bonds). It is a very stable structure.
A cylindrical fullerene, essentially a tube of graphene. A nanoparticle known for its strength and electrical conductivity.

blocks.text: Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon that have a giant structure. Graphite is made of layers of hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
Each layer of carbon atoms in graphite is called {graphene}. It is another allotrope of carbon: a sheet that is one atom thick.

items: A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings.
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others.

blocks.text: Like graphite, graphene has a giant structure, so:

items.title: High melting and boiling points
items.sub: strong covalent bonds need large amounts of energy to break

items.title: Conducts electricity
items.sub: each carbon atom gives one delocalised electron that can move and carry charge

blocks.text: Even though it is only one atom thick, graphene is very strong. The pattern of strong covalent bonds between the carbon atoms is unbroken.
Graphene is also very lightweight, flexible and practically transparent. That makes it useful in flexible electronics.

items.q: How many layers of carbon atoms does graphene have?
How many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom in graphene bonded to?

options: It has delocalised electrons that move and carry charge.
It has weak forces between its layers.
Its carbon atoms are delocalised and move.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: Graphene is not a multi-layered structure held together by weak forces. That describes graphite. Graphene has only one layer of carbon atoms, each atom held by strong covalent bonds.
They share properties because both have giant covalent structures: a high melting point and electrical conductivity.

items.title: Graphite
items.sub: a three-dimensional structure with weak forces between its layers. The layers slide over each other, so it can be a lubricant

items.title: Graphene
items.sub: a single layer. Extremely strong but also flexible, because every carbon atom is bonded to three others

blocks.text: Fullerenes are molecular allotropes of carbon. Each atom is covalently bonded to three others, forming hollow spheres or tubes.

items: Fullerenes have a defined number of atoms in their structure, so they are molecules.
They are simple molecular substances, not giant covalent structures.
The structure is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, or on rings of five or seven atoms.

blocks.label: How is C₆₀ written?
blocks.text: C₆₀ tells us that there are 60 carbon atoms in the molecule.
The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene. It has 60 carbon atoms.

items.title: Cage-like fused rings
items.sub: hexagons and pentagons, like a football

items.title: Three bonds each
items.sub: every carbon atom is bonded to three others

items: It is a black solid that dissolves in organic solvents to make a violet solution.
C₆₀ is the most stable fullerene.

blocks.text: C₂₀ is the smallest fullerene, but fullerenes can have hundreds, or potentially even thousands, of carbon atoms.
Fullerenes are made of rings of five and six carbon atoms, and sometimes seven.
Because they are simple molecules, fullerenes have low melting and boiling points. There are only weak forces between the molecules.
What makes fullerenes different from diamond, graphite and graphene? They are simple molecules and they form a closed, cage-like structure.
Each carbon atom in a fullerene has only three covalent bonds, so there is one extra electron per atom that is delocalised.
But spherical fullerenes are separate molecules. The electrons cannot move from one molecule to another, so **spherical fullerenes cannot conduct electricity**.

blocks.q: Which type of structure has each substance?

blocks.text: Cylindrical fullerenes are known as **carbon nanotubes**. A nanotube is effectively a sheet of graphene rolled into a cylinder.

items: They have a very high length to diameter ratio: they are very long compared to their width.
They have delocalised electrons that can move along the tube and carry a charge or current.
They have a very high tensile strength. This means they resist breaking or stretching.
They are also quite lightweight and flexible.

blocks.text: These properties make them useful in composites, specialised materials, electronics and nanotechnology.

blocks.q: Why can nanotubes conduct electricity when spherical fullerenes cannot?
options: Nanotubes are long structures, so electrons can move along them. Spherical fullerenes are separate molecules.
Spherical fullerenes have no delocalised electrons at all.
Nanotubes have weak forces between layers.
blocks.why: Spherical fullerenes do have delocalised electrons, but the electrons cannot move from one molecule to the next.

blocks.q: Why do fullerenes like C₆₀ have low melting points compared with graphene?
options: They are molecules with weak forces between them, so less energy is needed to change state.
They have weaker covalent bonds than graphene.
blocks.why: Fullerenes are discrete molecules held to each other by weak forces. Graphene has strong covalent bonds throughout that must all be broken to melt it.

blocks.q: Spherical fullerenes are described as slippery. Why?
options: Their shape lets them roll over each other easily, which reduces friction.
Their layers slide over each other.
blocks.why: Graphite is slippery because its layers slide. Spherical fullerenes are slippery because they roll over each other.

items: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, is very strong and conducts electricity.
Fullerenes are molecules of carbon with hollow shapes.
The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, or on carbon rings of five or seven atoms.
A Buckminsterfullerene is a spherical fullerene of sixty carbon atoms (C₆₀).
A carbon nanotube is a tube of graphene that is very long compared to its diameter and has a high tensile strength.

flashcards.back: A single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon atoms one atom thick, arranged in hexagonal rings.

flashcards.front: How many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to in graphene?

flashcards.back: Very strong, conducts electricity, and a high melting point. It is also lightweight, flexible and practically transparent.
Each carbon atom provides one delocalised electron that is free to move and carry a charge or current.
Molecular allotropes of carbon with hollow shapes: spheres or tubes.

flashcards.front: What are fullerene structures based on?
flashcards.back: Hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, and sometimes rings of five or seven atoms.
A spherical fullerene of 60 carbon atoms (C₆₀). It is very stable and is nicknamed buckyballs.
C₂₀, with 20 carbon atoms. Fullerenes can also have hundreds or even thousands.

flashcards.front: Why do fullerenes such as C₆₀ have low melting and boiling points?
flashcards.back: They are simple molecules with weak forces between the molecules, so not much energy is needed to change state.

flashcards.front: Why can spherical fullerenes not conduct electricity?
flashcards.back: They have delocalised electrons, but the electrons cannot move from one molecule to another.
A cylindrical fullerene: effectively a sheet of graphene rolled into a tube, very long compared with its diameter.

flashcards.front: What does high tensile strength mean?
flashcards.back: Resistant to breaking or stretching. Nanotubes have it.

flashcards.front: Give some uses of carbon nanotubes.
flashcards.back: Composites, specialised materials, electronics and nanotechnology.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Graphene and fullerenes
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word or a number.

questions.prompt: Graphene is a single layer of which allotrope of carbon?
questions.explanation: Each layer of carbon atoms in graphite is called graphene.

questions.prompt: How many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to in graphene? Write a number.
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom in graphene is covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings.

questions.prompt: What type of structure does graphene have: giant covalent or simple molecular?
questions.explanation: Graphene has strong covalent bonds throughout the sheet, so it is a giant covalent structure.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀? Write a number.
Buckminsterfullerene has a common nickname that starts with the letters b-u-c-k-y. What is it?
What type of structure does C₆₀ have: giant covalent or simple molecular?
questions.explanation: C₆₀ has a defined number of atoms, so it is a simple molecule.

questions.prompt: Does C₆₀ have a high or a low melting point? Answer with the word high or low.
questions.explanation: C₆₀ is a simple molecular substance with weak forces between its molecules.

questions.prompt: Can spherical fullerenes such as C₆₀ conduct electricity? Answer yes or no.
questions.explanation: Their delocalised electrons cannot move from one molecule to another.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a cylindrical fullerene?
questions.explanation: Cylindrical fullerenes are known as carbon nanotubes.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in C₂₀, the smallest fullerene? Write a number.
questions.explanation: The number in the formula is the number of carbon atoms, so C₂₀ has 20.
